Janice Honeyman

By: Hein Kaiser | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We celebrate one of South Africa's most inspiring entertainment personalities, the Queen of the Pantomime, Janice Honeyman

Unique Selling Point:
For the past 35 years Janice Honeyman has signaled the festive season with her unforgettable pantomimes. Its a genre all on its own, a feel good formula where good always triumphs over evil in the end. It has brough lightness and fun to South African families.



Summary:
Juxtaposed to that is Honeyman's serious side. She has produced and or directed some of South Africa's most groundbreaking theatre too. The edgy musical Hair, long banned for its nude scenes and psychedelic undertones, and The Colour Purple with themes of humanity, decimation of human rights and darkness we all carry.

It's a celebration of a theatrical shape-shifter, an entertainer that on the one hand made us laugh and sing for decades, while at her opposite, made us think and explore ourselves.

Further information:
We will be talking to a couple of cast members and crew who have worked with Honeyman over the years, to share with us what its like to work with her. Also, a current cast member from Peter Pan, her current panto, and a Honeyman debutante.

VO: It’s a genre of theatre easily dismissed as frivolous, a bit of meaningless escapism. But, in the chaos and confusion of our times, Pantomime might just be the perfect theatrical antidote: providing much-needed respite from the burden of modern life.

VO: And there are few, if any, as skilled in the genre as Janice Honeyman, theatre impresario and the unofficial “queen of pantomime”.

[00:02:01] There are always funny moments in a pantomime. They were always incredible moments.


VO: In this world, good always triumphs over evil and happy endings are mandatory - quite unlike the daily South African reality. And so, with Pantomime season in full swing, it’s appropriate to catch up with someone whose rich and varied career in the theatre has held up a mirror to a complex and challenged society, one that occasionally needs to cut loose and have a laugh.

**END OF INTRO SEQUENCE - NEEDS A TRANSITION**


VO: Janice has her mother to thank for her love of stories. One Christmas, she gave her daughter a copy of Anne of Green Gables which Janice read eleven times.

Even so, it wasn’t immediately obvious that she’d follow a career on - and off - the stage. But, she was passionate about literature and seemed destined for a life in the arts.

JANICE
[14:23:53] I studied drama at drama school, became a professional actress, and went up to the Transvaal, what was then the Transvaal to Pact and lived in Pretoria for four years.


VO: Pact, or the Performing Arts Council of the old Transvaal, was a provincial government arts department employing actors and directors.

Among them was an actor who would later work extensively with Janice and himself become a household name, Tobie Cronje. In those early days, Janice, too, was an actor.

TOBIE
00:08:14] Janice and I went ice skating. But we, of course, weren't allowed to do because you might get hurt. And lo and behold, Janis was holding my hand while she was skating around. And she fell. And we laughed. And I said, Oh, get up. And she said, I can't have broken my leg. And she really did. She broke her leg.


JANICE
[14:24:12] I couldn't walk for eight months. And the Mannny Mahn who started the Market Theater but was still at PACT in those days said, You're not going to sit on your bum for eight months. His schools program, his library program and his children's play. And he said, you're going to direct them. And I did. And I thought, this is much nicer than being an actor. So that sort of started it all.


VO: Fate had intervened and Janice moved from acting into directing… and sometimes both. A career that coincided with theatre’s increasing relevance in a turbulent country.
P1044394
UPS JANICE
[14:38:15] Theater in this country changed the attitude to life, changed the attitude to apartheid, to integration, to all of those things we were struggling with. Theatre did it. And I think that it can be a very powerful medium.


JANICE
[14:33:12] I do opera, I do musicals, I do serious musicals. I do frivolous musicals. I do pantomime, and I do straight drama. And in fact, I'm happy when I'm doing really serious drama. But it is each one is a different technique.

VO: In 1976 when the Market Theatre opened in downtown Jozi, Janice joined as a founding member.

The home of protest theatre, the eighties saw them contending with severe government censorship as Apartheid security police targeted their productions.


JANICE
[14:40:33] Holy Moses and all that jazz, which was a sweet little biblical musical story. Adam and Eve Center and what's his name, said various one little cantatas that they did at schools. And they said this was irreligious and blasphemous and and the whole lot of saints would came. And they said at the interview there was the lawyer, their lawyer was looking into a glass case at the at the market. And I sat down and I said, so what do you think? Which is cheeky. But yeah. And he said, Well, I'm really loving it. I don't know what to say. It was able to say anything in it and they did get it that. And it was they said because a they reasons with holy Moses is swearing blaspheming and all that jazz an audience would expect music and said there is no jazz in there. It's not jazz so you lying to the public and that's why we banning you


VO: Then, in the new South Africa, protest theatre made way for more nuanced - but no less difficult - storytelling.


XOLA
[14:29:53] What are the biggest challenges you've come across?
JANICE
(14:30:17] I think the biggest challenge is the two challenges. One is to keep up to date and in touch, and the other is to do as much as you can with integration.


JANICE
[14:30:31] the Color Purple, for instance, it was completely black and. I had to learn. How you relate in that way, because we all grew up with apartheid and it was a difficult, difficult crossover to make.


VO: Janice has faced her share of critics, accusing her of cultural appropriation.


JANICE
[14:31:07] you could say that to me if I was doing a Chekhov, because I do. I understand the Russian culture. I learn about it. And that because one's working on human nature most of the time. That's what you identify with people in a different way are. All the same. Heart wise, they are all the same.


VO: It’s a commitment to our shared humanity - and a love of stories - that fuels her approach to every theatre genre… yes, even pantomime.
